answer: According to the AI risk taxonomy summary, teams should classify risks into capability, misuse, alignment, and systemic categories. This helps prioritize controls based on deployment context and communicate consistently about severity.

Based on evaluation guidance, benchmark scores measure narrow behavior slices and do not guarantee safe production deployment. Teams should combine benchmarks with domain-specific golden evals and human review.
Model governance should include approval workflows, version pinning, rollback plans, and audit trails. High-impact deployments require documented decisions and evidence from evals before launch.
Grounding reduces hallucination risk by tying answers to approved sources, using citation checks, and failing closed when evidence is missing. Teams should measure grounding with golden evals.
According to red-team guidance, testing proactively searches for jailbreaks and unsafe completions using adversarial prompts. Teams should repeat exercises after major model or prompt changes.
AI safety is mostly about buying the newest model. Benchmarks guarantee safety so governance is optional.
Hallucinations are certainly safe when using retrieval. Benchmark scores are guaranteed safe in all deployments.
Red team testing is unnecessary. Governance is certainly safe to skip and deploy immediately.
Risk taxonomies are useful but details depend on context.
Evals help track regressions, but teams still need grounding checks and human review for high-stakes tasks.
